The submission reads as a sincere but unvalidated concept. The most valuable improvements, in priority order:

1. Replace assumptions with evidence. The plan relies on vague claims ('a meaningful number,' 'a large number of families,' 'a small number of parents we know personally'). Run a structured customer discovery effort (30-50 interviews or a survey of 100+ parents) and report concrete findings: how often parents check labels, what they do today, what they would pay, and which pain point is sharpest (packaged snacks vs. school menus). Replace the vague market claims with sourced data (e.g., CDC or FARE prevalence figures) and a bottom-up TAM/SAM/SOM estimate with explicit assumptions.

2. Show proof of progress. There is no prototype, website, landing page, or pilot. Before resubmitting, build a minimal demo (even a basic OCR-plus-allergen-matching proof of concept), a clickable mockup, or a waitlist landing page with signup counts. Even 20-50 committed pilot families or letters of interest would materially strengthen credibility.

3. Address accuracy, liability, and trust directly. This is the largest omitted risk. A false 'safe' result on an allergen app can cause serious harm. The plan should explain how OCR errors, ambiguous ingredient names, cross-contamination labels, and recipe changes will be handled; what the accuracy target and testing method are; how disclaimers, insurance, and an LLC liability structure apply; and whether regulatory or privacy issues arise (children's data, COPPA, app store health policies). Include the plan to validate the allergen knowledge base with clinicians or allergists.

4. Clarify the technical approach and feasibility. Explain how school menus will actually be handled, since menus often list dish names rather than ingredients. Where would ingredient data come from (product databases, district nutrition data, manual lookup)? Specify the data sources, OCR approach, and the realistic accuracy limits. This is likely the core differentiator, yet it is currently asserted rather than demonstrated.

5. Sharpen competitive analysis. Name specific competitors (e.g., Yuka, Fig, Spokin, Spoonful, Content Checked-type tools), compare features in a table, and state concretely what they lack for the school-lunch use case. 'Focus on families' is not a defensible moat; identify one (proprietary school menu data, district partnerships, brand trust, accuracy record) and explain how it compounds over time.

6. Build a real business model. Provide a price point with justification, benchmark against comparable subscription apps, and state conversion and churn assumptions. Include a simple unit-economics view (customer acquisition cost, lifetime value, cloud/OCR cost per scan) and a one- to three-year projection with explicit assumptions. Either develop or cut the speculative revenue streams (brand partnerships, school licensing); also consider whether brand partnerships create a trust conflict for an app whose value is neutral safety guidance.

7. Define a go-to-market plan. Specify how the first 500-1,000 users will be reached: allergy parent communities and Facebook groups, advocacy organizations, pediatric allergists, school nurses, PTAs. Explain why parents would trust a new student-run app with their child's safety, and what partnerships or endorsements would address that.

8. Make the ask and milestones concrete. 'Several thousand dollars' is not a budget. Provide an itemized use of funds (development, cloud costs, legal/insurance, testing), a timeline with measurable milestones (prototype by month X, pilot with N families by month Y, accuracy of Z% on a test set), and the success metrics that would justify further investment.

9. Strengthen the team narrative. The mix of technical, business, and public health skills is a real strength, so highlight it with specifics (relevant projects, coursework, family experience). Acknowledge gaps honestly (no consumer product experience, no clinical advisor, no industry contacts) and name the advisors or mentors you will recruit to fill them, ideally with at least one allergist or dietitian committed before resubmission.

10. Tighten the writing. The tone is clear and honest, but heavy use of hedging ('we believe,' 'we hope,' 'we are still deciding') weakens persuasiveness. Convert hedges into specific hypotheses with planned tests, lead with a one-sentence value proposition and traction, and add a short 'key risks and mitigations' section. Honesty about unknowns is good; pair each with a concrete plan and date to resolve it.
